passage: Coach's note, Saturday under-10 practice, Thomas D'Souza. Since last week's news story about a boy struck by lightning at a football ground in another state, eleven of fourteen parents have asked me to cancel practice whenever there are clouds. Today the sky was grey but calm, and six kids stayed home. Meanwhile, I counted: four children arrived on the back of two-wheelers without helmets, and one car came through the gate fast while kids were crossing. Nobody has mentioned either once in the parents' group. The lightning story was on every channel for three days. Next: I'll keep our storm rule as it is (thunder heard, everyone inside), and at pickup I'll raise helmets and gate speed with the parents, starting with Chinmay's family, who drive the carpool.

qa.q: How many of the fourteen parents asked to cancel practice when there are clouds?
qa.a: Eleven of fourteen parents.

qa.q: What seems to worry Thomas most, judging by what Thomas chose to count?
qa.a: Thomas seems more worried about everyday dangers, like rides without helmets and a car speeding through the gate, than the rare lightning risk the parents fear.

qa.q: What did Thomas decide to do next, and why is it a balanced choice?
qa.a: Thomas kept the existing storm rule and planned to raise helmets and gate speed at pickup, which respects the parents' fear while pointing them to the common risks.

qa.q: Why might the parents feel the lightning story is more urgent than the helmets?
qa.a: The story was vivid and on every channel for days, so it feels close and frightening, while helmetless rides are so ordinary nobody notices them.

grounding: A coach notes parents panicking about a rare lightning risk after one news story, while everyday traffic risks go unmentioned.

passage:
Sunday night
The colony has gone a bit mad. Ever since that TV story about a child snatched from a park in another city, the parents' group has talked about nothing else. Naveen bhai wants cameras on every tree. Kids aren't allowed in the park now, even with parents. Mrs Kapoor has hired a guard for the gate.
Meanwhile the open drain by Gate 2 still has no cover. Two kids fell into it last monsoon. Scooters still race down the lane at school time. I mentioned both in the group. One thumbs-up. Then eighty messages about the park.
I get it. That story was terrifying. But the drain is actually here, on our lane.
— Farhan

qa.q: What still has no cover by Gate 2?
qa.a: The open drain.

qa.q: What does Farhan feel about the colony's reaction?
qa.a: Farhan understands the fear, since the story was terrifying, but is frustrated that everyday dangers like the drain get one thumbs-up while the park gets eighty messages.

qa.q: What could Farhan try next so the drain gets attention?
qa.a: Farhan could raise it with Naveen bhai directly or at a meeting, mentioning the two kids who fell in, rather than only posting in the busy group.

qa.q: How might the children in the colony experience the new rules?
qa.a: The children lose the park, even with parents, while still walking past an open drain and fast scooters, so they are less free without being much safer.

grounding: A resident's diary notes the colony panicking over a rare kidnapping story while an open drain and speeding scooters are ignored.

passage: After a news channel showed a leopard attack in a district two hundred kilometres away, Dhanori changed overnight. Preeti watched it happen from the door of her anganwadi near the temple. Parents stopped letting children walk the field path to school, even at noon. Vijay, the sarpanch's son, organised men with sticks to guard the path and had an announcement made on the loudspeaker twice a day. Nobody in Dhanori had seen a leopard in living memory. Meanwhile, every evening, sugarcane tractor-trolleys roared down the main road with no back lights, and boys still rode on top of the loads, waving. Preeti mentioned the trolleys at the panchayat meeting. Vijay nodded politely and went back to the leopard.

qa.q: Who organised men with sticks to guard the path?
qa.a: Vijay, the sarpanch's son, organised them.

qa.q: What might Preeti be worried about when she raises the trolleys at the meeting?
qa.a: She seems worried that the everyday danger of unlit, overloaded trolleys is being ignored while everyone fears a leopard no one has seen.

qa.q: How could Preeti make her point about the trolleys land better?
qa.a: She could describe a concrete near-miss on the main road and suggest one simple step, like back lights, instead of arguing against the leopard fear.

qa.a: The vivid TV story feels urgent and gives him a visible way to protect people, while the trolleys are familiar and feel normal.

passage: Beatriz had lived on Keurboom Street in Cape Town for two years when the tree story arrived. A storm in another city had dropped an old pine onto a parked car, and the video ran on every news site for days. By the weekend, the residents' association wanted every old tree on the street cut down. Lindiwe from number 14 went door to door with a petition, and people signed fast, still talking about the crushed car. Beatriz signed nothing. She stood at the corner with her coffee and watched the school run: cars speeding down the hill, children dashing across where the pedestrian light had been broken since March. Nobody had petitioned about that. She took a photo of the dead light and wondered who would even look at it.

qa.q: How long had the pedestrian light been broken?
qa.a: It had been broken since March.

qa.q: What was Beatriz feeling as she watched the school run?
qa.a: She seemed uneasy and a bit frustrated that a far-off video had everyone's attention while a daily danger outside was ignored.

qa.q: What could Beatriz do with her photo of the broken light?
qa.a: She could share it with the residents' association and ask Lindiwe to add the crossing to the petition, turning attention to the common risk.

qa.q: How might Lindiwe see the petition differently from Beatriz?
qa.a: Lindiwe probably sees it as protecting neighbours from a real danger shown on the news, not as over-caution.

grounding: An adult watches a vivid story about a rare accident drive the street's caution while an everyday risk goes unfixed.

passage:
Nandini had been the nurse at the primary school for two years. On Monday, a TV channel showed a story about a child in another state who was bitten by a rare venomous spider in a school garden.
By Wednesday, parents were at the gate demanding the garden be closed. Sonali, the principal, agreed and had it locked. Some parents stopped sending children to outdoor PE altogether.
Nandini watched it all with a sinking feeling. In two years she had treated zero spider bites. She had treated forty scraped knees from the broken tiles near the staircase, and three children hit by speeding bikes at the school gate, where there was still no crossing guard.
Nobody at the meeting mentioned the gate or the tiles. Everyone was talking about spiders.

qa.q: How many spider bites had Nandini treated in two years?
qa.a: She had treated zero spider bites.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling as she watched parents demand the garden be closed?
qa.a: Nandini felt uneasy and frustrated, with a sinking feeling, knowing the real everyday risks were being ignored.

qa.q: What could Nandini do at the next parents' meeting?
qa.a: She could share her records of scraped knees and bike injuries and suggest fixing the tiles and getting a crossing guard.

qa.q: How might Sonali, the principal, see the situation?
qa.a: Sonali probably feels pressured by worried parents and relieved to act quickly, without noticing the more common risks.

grounding: A school nurse watches one dramatic news story push parents into over-caution about spiders while common risks like broken tiles and traffic are ignored.

passage:
Subject: About the lift ban
Dear Sahil,
As RWA president you've been flooded with messages, so I'll keep this short.
After the news video of a lift falling in another city, our building voted to stop using lifts. Now Mr Kulkarni, who's eighty-two, is climbing seven floors with his cane, and the Deshpandes carry their baby up and down every day.
I understand the fear. That video was terrifying. But our lifts were inspected last month and passed.
What worries me more: the stair lights on floors three and five have been broken for weeks, and the stairs are wet from the leak. More of us will slip on those stairs than will ever be in a lift accident.
Can we fix the lights and talk about this calmly on Sunday?
Nikita

qa.q: When were the building's lifts last inspected?
qa.a: Our lifts were inspected last month and passed.

qa.q: What is Nikita feeling while writing this email?
qa.a: Nikita feels worried and a bit frustrated, seeing a rare event drive the building's choices while real dangers are ignored.

qa.q: What does Nikita suggest, and why is it wiser?
qa.a: Nikita suggests fixing the stair lights and talking calmly, because broken lights and wet stairs are a more common risk than lift accidents.

qa.q: How might Mr Kulkarni be affected by the lift ban?
qa.a: Mr Kulkarni, at eighty-two with a cane, has to climb seven floors, which is exhausting and risky for him.

grounding: A resident sees one dramatic news video push the building into avoiding lifts while common everyday risks are ignored.

passage:
Binita, you asked about our colony's "snake summer". I'm Tejas, and I watched the whole thing happen.
One evening a local news channel ran a story about a cobra found in a house in another town. It went viral. Suddenly our colony group was full of snake photos from everywhere. People started pouring kerosene around their gates. Parents stopped kids playing in the park. Someone called a snake catcher for a garden hose.
Meanwhile, the real problem nobody talked about: the colony road with no speed breakers, where bikes race past the school bus stop every morning. Two kids had been hit there that year. No snakes had ever been seen in our colony.
I raised it at the meeting. Everyone nodded, then went back to talking about snakes.

qa.q: What did someone call a snake catcher for?
qa.a: Someone called a snake catcher for a garden hose.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when everyone went back to talking about snakes?
qa.a: Tejas felt frustrated and a little helpless, knowing the real danger on the road was being ignored.

qa.q: What could Tejas try next to shift the colony's focus?
qa.a: Tejas could gather the facts about the two children hit on the road and ask the colony to write to the municipality for speed breakers.

qa.q: How might the parents who stopped kids playing in the park see things?
qa.a: They probably feel protective and frightened, doing what seems safest after the viral story, without noticing the road risk.

grounding: A resident watches one viral snake story push the colony into over-caution while a common road danger is ignored.

I'm Ujjwal, and I live on the second floor, so I see our colony lane every day. After a TV channel ran a dramatic story about a child snatched from a park in another city, our colony changed overnight. Parents stopped sending kids to the park at all. Damini, from the flat opposite, put up a notice about strangers and started a night-watch group. I can't know what everyone felt, but the lane went strangely quiet.
What didn't change: delivery bikes still raced through our narrow lane, and kids still ran across it to buy chips. On Thursday a scooter clipped a boy's elbow. I walked him home to his mother, who took him to the clinic. Nobody put up a notice about that.

qa.q: What clipped a boy's elbow on Thursday?
qa.a: A scooter.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling as the lane went quiet?
qa.a: Ujjwal seemed uneasy and puzzled, watching fear of a rare event grow while a daily danger was ignored.

qa.q: What could the colony do about the everyday risk?

qa.a: They may feel bored and confused, kept indoors because of a story from another city.

Monday: A news video showed a lift falling in a building in another city. By evening, Ankita's building group was buzzing. Damini, the secretary, wrote: "Nobody use the lift till further notice!"
Wednesday: Elderly residents panted up six floors with groceries. Mr Bose from 5B nearly fell on the dark stairwell, where the bulb had been dead for months. The lift itself had passed its safety check in March; the certificate was pinned by the door, but nobody mentioned it.
The next Sunday: Ankita counted three dead stair bulbs, a loose railing and wet tiles near the tank. She wrote in the group: "The lift passed its check. The stairs haven't." Damini replied, "Let's fix the lights first."

passage:
Anand, everyone in your office is scared of flying since that crash on the news? Let your Madhuri bua tell you something. When I was twenty-five, a newspaper printed a big photo of a cobra found in a baby's cradle in some faraway town. For weeks our whole mohalla shook out every sheet, every shoe, every cradle, twice a night. Mothers barely slept.
Meanwhile the open drain at the end of our lane had no cover, and children played on its edge every day. I watched it and said nothing, because I was scared of snakes too. Then one monsoon a little boy slipped in; thank God the vegetable seller pulled him out. Only then did the mohalla fix the drain cover. One photo moved us more than the danger we saw every day.

qa.q: Who pulled the boy out of the drain?
qa.a: The vegetable seller.

qa.q: What was young Madhuri feeling during those weeks?
qa.a: She felt scared along with everyone, even while noticing the open drain nobody worried about.

qa.q: What choice in the story could have come sooner?
qa.a: Covering the drain, the everyday danger, instead of only checking sheets for a rare snake.

qa.q: How might the mothers of the mohalla have felt during those weeks?
qa.a: They were anxious and exhausted, barely sleeping while shaking out sheets for a rare danger.

grounding: An aunt recalls watching a single dramatic news photo drive her neighbourhood into over-caution about a rare danger while a common one was ignored.

'Did you see the video, Rajni? A dog bit a child in some colony in Hyderabad!'
'I saw it, Zeenat Apa.'
'Now the association wants every street dog in our lane taken away. They've called the municipal van.'
'Has any dog here ever bitten anyone?'
'No, but you saw the video!'
'I saw it. I also saw the delivery boys doing sixty down our lane this morning, and the Sharma boy on his cycle with no lights.'
'That's different.'
'How many children have been hurt by bikes here this year?'
Zeenat paused. 'Two. Little Farzana's leg.'
'And by dogs?'
'None.' Zeenat frowned at her phone. 'But the video is so scary.'
'It is,' said Rajni gently. 'That's why it's all anyone talks about.'

qa.q: How many children had been hurt by bikes in the lane that year, according to Zeenat?
qa.a: Two.

qa.a: Rajni seemed calm but concerned, worried that one scary video was pulling attention from the lane's real dangers.

qa.q: What could the association do instead of focusing only on the dogs?
qa.a: It could look at what has actually hurt children in the lane, like speeding bikes, and act on that too, for example by asking for speed breakers.

qa.q: How does Zeenat's view change during the talk?
qa.a: Zeenat starts out alarmed by the video, then pauses when she remembers Farzana's leg, though she still finds the video frightening.

passage: I'm Kashish, and I've been watching my colony for a month now. It started with one news story from another city: a child snatched from a park. Horrible, and rare. But it was shared everywhere. Within days, parents here stopped letting children play in our park, even in daylight. My neighbour Lakshmi, who used to sit on the bench chatting, now keeps her daughter indoors. There's a new colony group just for "suspicious people". Meanwhile, every morning, the same children are driven through the main road crossing, where cars speed and there's no zebra line. Two scooters collided there last week. Nobody posted about that. I don't blame anyone for being scared. I just see the fear pointing at the wrong thing.
